title: Aftersun's treatment of memory and representation, and why it's one of my favourite films of the century

commenti.body:
easily my fav film of the 2020s so far, its already sitting in the 5th spot for my fav films, full stop.

So much naunce to the work I pick up new things every time. The fact that its basically an autobiographical piece for the director makes it all the more poignant.

Shockbomb for me and def top 5 movie experience.
As an only child who supported melancholy separated parents during childhood, the movie was so excellent at conveying this experience, notably the misery of pretending to have fun in whatever has been organised by your solo parent to prevent them from psychically crumbling.

A true modern masterpiece, an outstanding bit of filmmaking and the fact the it was a debut feature is incredible. No film has captured the warmth and pains  of memory and with such incredible detail. One of the finest endings I have ever seen.

My take is that the movie is about that time and place where our sheltered existences are shattered. Sophie is 11, she thinks she’s grown up enough to play with the kids, but she’s also not mature enough to mingle with the group of teens she meets at the resort. She’s first experiencing more complex thoughts and feelings, but she can’t fully understand them. She can see flashes of her father not only in the role of “Dad”, but also as an adult with his own emotional baggage. Sophie, at 11, could never get a full picture, just as the director is unable to do so. It’s clear that the father had a lot of trauma to process, but he tried to keep everything in check (through practicing tai chi, for instance) to prevent his daughter of getting to know the worst in him.

She goes back to the family movies in an attempt to understand her father, but the movies only got the good moments. The scene where he asks her to put the camera down and then tells her about an episode of his abusive childhood is incredible, because the director keeps focused on the TV set in the hotel room, where we see the reflections of Sophie and her dad. It implies that the most important moments in our lives aren’t “registered” as meaningful while they are happening, because we can only appreciate them as such with the distance of time. Just like playing pool and going for a dive seem mundane and commonplace - and that’s why the movie ignores narrative structures and dedicates so much of its running time to the recreations of seemingly unremarkable events. 

That’s also why many people watch Aftersun and think nothing happens in this movie; those are people that were trained by other movies to expect a certain kind of character arc, and this movie subverts all expectations. Sophie’s parents are no longer together, and we anticipate this could be a conflict in the movie; it’s not, because they care about here and have a civil relationship. We expect Sophie will get in trouble when she gets closer to the group of teens in the hotel; yet the teens treat her with respect and care. We think the father and daughter relationship will be damaged after an argument, but everything is settled the next day with an apology.

It's important that we get to experience their relationship in the most naturalistic terms, because that makes us feel like we're Sophie, and we feel like we're sent back to those times when life was simple and we lived in a world that was still protected by parents that, despite their personal demons, were doing their best to keep us safe and comforted. That's what the memory of her father ultimately means.

To this day I still have a fear of others thinking i'll be disappointed about gifts and events. As someone who had depressed separated parents take me on package holidays (including one to the same Turkish mud bath as in the film) and has suffered heavy from depression my entire adult life I have never felt a film so perfectly capture my experience. 

Somewhat off topic since the main focus of this thread is Sophie but the final scene in the airport when after she's gone he just sags is the perfect capture of that empty feeling after what should have been a great time, makes me want to cry just thinking about it.

Kazuo Ishiguro said that memory has a texture that's impossible to replicate in film. Well, I think Aftersun did the impossible.

Callum is hardly tangible in the film. When he cries, we only see his back. When they sing a song for his birthday, we only see his outline in the sunlight haze. When he speaks about his sad childhood, we see him reflected on the dead TV screen. It culminates in the nightclub scene, a liminal space, non-reality. Callum spits on his reflection too and that scene cut deep for me. Old clips are interwoven into the cinematography, a constant reminder that we're remembering with Sophie, that what's unfolding isn't happening in real-time.

Callum said that each rug tells a story, and he is a mosaic of memories. A fading one as Sophie tries to understand his Dad one last time as she's now the same age as he was at the time.

It was never clear what happened to Callum although suicide is the strongest implication...
